title: Chemical Equilibrium: Reversible Reactions and Dynamic Equilibrium
summary: Reversible and irreversible reactions, how equilibrium is reached and why it is dynamic, and Le Chatelier's principle.

p: An irreversible reaction goes to completion and the products do not change back under the same conditions. Example: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. Once magnesium has burned, the oxide does not break down again.

A reversible reaction can go in both directions. We write it with a double arrow (⇌). Example: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g). Nitrogen and hydrogen form ammonia, but ammonia also breaks down into nitrogen and hydrogen.

At the start there are many reactant particles, so the forward reaction is fast. As reactants are used up and products build up, the reverse reaction speeds up. Eventually the forward and reverse rates become equal. From then on the concentrations of reactants and products do not change. This state is chemical equilibrium.

Equilibrium is dynamic, not static: the particles are still reacting in both directions, but at the same rate, so nothing seems to change. Equilibrium can only be reached in a closed system (one from which nothing escapes).

img.alt: A balance showing the rate of the forward reaction equal to the rate of the reverse reaction at dynamic equilibrium
img.cap: At equilibrium the two rates are equal.

p: Irreversible: goes to completion; arrow →; cannot be reversed under the same conditions; example 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. Reversible: does not go to completion; arrow ⇌; both reactants and products are present at equilibrium; example N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃.
If a change is made to a system at equilibrium, the position of equilibrium shifts to oppose the change.

Concentration: adding a reactant shifts the equilibrium to the right (forward); adding a product shifts it to the left. Pressure (gases): increasing the pressure shifts the equilibrium to the side with fewer moles of gas. Temperature: raising the temperature favours the endothermic direction; lowering it favours the exothermic direction. Catalyst: speeds up both directions equally, so equilibrium is reached sooner, but the position does not change.

Haber process: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, ΔH = −92 kJ/mol. High pressure (about 200 atm) favours ammonia (4 moles of gas become 2). A low temperature would favour ammonia (exothermic), but it would be too slow, so about 450 °C is used with an iron catalyst. Contact process: 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃ with a vanadium(V) oxide catalyst.
Haber process (ammonia for fertilisers); Contact process (sulphuric acid); carbonated drinks (CO₂ dissolved ⇌ CO₂ gas above the liquid); oxygen binding to haemoglobin in blood.

title: The Equilibrium Constant Kc and Calculations
summary: Writing the expression for Kc, what its size means, factors that do and do not change it, and worked calculations.

p: For a reversible reaction aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD at equilibrium, Kc = [C]ᶜ[D]ᵈ / ([A]ᵃ[B]ᵇ). The square brackets mean concentration in mol/dm³ at equilibrium. Products go on top and reactants at the bottom; the coefficients become powers. Solids and pure liquids are left out.
Examples. 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃: Kc = [SO₃]² / ([SO₂]²[O₂]). N₂O₄ ⇌ 2NO₂: Kc = [NO₂]² / [N₂O₄].

sections.h: What the size of Kc tells us
p: Kc depends only on temperature. A large Kc (much greater than 1) means that the equilibrium mixture contains mostly products. A small Kc (much less than 1) means that it contains mostly reactants. If Kc is about 1, there are comparable amounts of both. Kc has no units when the number of moles of reactants equals that of products; otherwise it has units that you can work out from the expression.
H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g). At equilibrium [H₂] = 0.2, [I₂] = 0.2 and [HI] = 0.6 mol/dm³. Kc = [HI]² / ([H₂][I₂]) = 0.6² / (0.2 × 0.2) = 0.36 / 0.04 = 9.0 (no units).
N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g). At equilibrium [N₂] = 0.1, [H₂] = 0.3, [NH₃] = 0.4 mol/dm³. Kc = 0.4² / (0.1 × 0.3³) = 0.16 / 0.0027 = 59.3 (units: mol⁻² dm⁶).
Another: H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI at 500 K with [H₂] = 0.1, [I₂] = 0.1, [HI] = 0.8: Kc = 0.64 / 0.01 = 64.

1.0 mol of H₂ and 1.0 mol of I₂ are placed in a 1 dm³ flask and Kc = 9. Let x mol of each react. At equilibrium [H₂] = [I₂] = 1 − x and [HI] = 2x. Kc = 4x² / (1 − x)² = 9, so 2x / (1 − x) = 3, 2x = 3 − 3x and x = 0.6. Equilibrium: [H₂] = [I₂] = 0.4 mol/dm³ and [HI] = 1.2 mol/dm³. Check: 1.2² / (0.4 × 0.4) = 1.44 / 0.16 = 9 ✓.

sections.h: What changes Kc and what does not
p: Temperature changes Kc. For an exothermic reaction, a rise in temperature decreases Kc. For an endothermic reaction, a rise in temperature increases Kc. Changes in concentration or pressure shift the position of equilibrium but do not change Kc. A catalyst does not change Kc.

Note on the Haber process: at room temperature Kc for ammonia is very large, but the reaction is far too slow. At 450 °C Kc is much smaller, which is why high pressure is also used to raise the yield.

title: Chemical Kinetics: Rate of Reaction and Factors
summary: What kinetics is, how rate is measured, collision theory, and the factors that change the rate of a reaction.

p: Chemical kinetics is the study of how fast reactions happen and by what steps. Thermodynamics tells us whether a reaction can happen; kinetics tells us how quickly. The rusting of iron is possible but slow. The burning of petrol is possible and fast.

The rate of reaction is the change in concentration of a reactant or product per unit time. For a reactant the rate is written with a minus sign, because its concentration falls: rate = −Δ[reactant]/Δt. For a product it is +Δ[product]/Δt. Units: mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹.

For 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂: rate = −(1/2) d[H₂O₂]/dt = d[O₂]/dt. The average rate is the change over a time interval; the instantaneous rate is the rate at one moment (the slope of the tangent to the concentration-time graph).
For a reaction to occur, particles must collide. Not every collision is effective. An effective collision needs (1) energy at least equal to the activation energy Eₐ and (2) the correct orientation.

1. Concentration: more particles in each volume means more frequent collisions, so the rate is higher. 2. Temperature: particles move faster and a larger fraction has energy of at least Eₐ. As a rough rule, the rate about doubles for every 10 °C rise. 3. Pressure (gases): more pressure means a higher concentration. 4. Surface area: powder reacts faster than lumps, because more particles are exposed. 5. Catalyst: provides another pathway with lower activation energy and is not used up (MnO₂ with H₂O₂). 6. Nature of reactants: ionic reactions such as neutralisation are very fast; reactions that break strong covalent bonds are slow.

title: Rate Laws and Order of Reaction
summary: The rate law, rate constant and order of reaction, how to find the order from experimental data, and first-order half-life calculations.

p: For A + B → products, the rate law is rate = k[A]ᵐ[B]ⁿ. k is the rate constant (it depends on temperature and catalyst, not on concentration). m and n are the orders with respect to A and B. m + n is the overall order. The rate law must be found by experiment; it cannot be read from the balanced equation.
Example: if rate = k[NO]²[O₂] for 2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂, then the order with respect to NO is 2, with respect to O₂ is 1 and the overall order is 3.

Zero order: the rate does not depend on concentration; rate = k (decomposition of NH₃ on hot tungsten). First order: rate = k[A] (radioactive decay, decomposition of N₂O₅). Second order: rate = k[A]² or k[A][B]. Orders can also be fractions.

sections.h: Finding the order: the method of initial rates
p: Measure the initial rate for different starting concentrations. Suppose:
Experiment 1: [A] = 0.1, [B] = 0.1, rate = 2.0 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹. Experiment 2: [A] = 0.2, [B] = 0.1, rate = 4.0 × 10⁻³. Experiment 3: [A] = 0.2, [B] = 0.2, rate = 16 × 10⁻³.

From 1 to 2, [A] doubles and the rate doubles: first order in A. From 2 to 3, [B] doubles and the rate is four times as large: second order in B. So rate = k[A][B]². Then k = 2.0 × 10⁻³ / (0.1 × 0.1²) = 2.0 dm⁶ mol⁻² s⁻¹. The units of k depend on the overall order.
Zero order: concentration against time is a straight line. First order: ln[A] against time is a straight line. Second order: 1/[A] against time is a straight line.
The half-life t½ is the time for the concentration to fall to half. For a first-order reaction it is constant: t½ = 0.693 / k.
Example. A first-order reaction has t½ = 300 s and [A]₀ = 1.0 mol/dm³. k = 0.693 / 300 = 2.31 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹. After 600 s (two half-lives) the concentration is 1.0 → 0.5 → 0.25 mol/dm³.
It helps to find reaction mechanisms, to understand how medicines break down in the body and to control industrial processes such as the Haber process, the Contact process and catalytic cracking.

title: Heat of Reaction and Enthalpy Change
summary: Thermochemistry: heat of reaction, enthalpy change ΔH, exothermic and endothermic reactions, types of heat of reaction and a calorimetry calculation.

p: Chemical reactions give out or take in heat. Thermochemistry is the study of these heat changes. It helps to predict whether reactions will happen, to design industrial processes, to find the energy needed in factories and to understand energy changes in living things.

Enthalpy (H) is the heat content of a system at constant pressure. The enthalpy change is ΔH = H(products) − H(reactants), in kJ per mole. ΔH is a state function: it depends only on the starting and finishing states, not on the route.

Exothermic reaction: heat is given out, ΔH is negative, and the temperature of the surroundings rises (burning methane, neutralisation, respiration). Endothermic reaction: heat is taken in, ΔH is positive, and the surroundings get cooler (photosynthesis, thermal decomposition of CaCO₃, dissolving ammonium chloride).
Heat of formation: the heat change when one mole of a compound is formed from its elements under standard conditions (25 °C, 1 atm). C(s) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g), ΔH = −394 kJ/mol.
Heat of combustion: the heat change when one mole of a substance burns completely in oxygen. CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l), ΔH = −890 kJ/mol.
Heat of neutralisation: the heat change when one mole of water is formed from an acid and a base. HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O, ΔH = −57 kJ/mol.
Heat of solution: the heat change when one mole of a substance dissolves in a large amount of solvent. Heat of atomisation: the heat needed to turn one mole of a substance into gaseous atoms.

50 cm³ of 1.0 mol/dm³ HCl is mixed with 50 cm³ of 1.0 mol/dm³ NaOH and the temperature rises by 6.8 °C. Find the heat of neutralisation. (Specific heat capacity of the solution = 4.2 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹; density = 1 g/cm³.) Heat produced q = m c ΔT = 100 × 4.2 × 6.8 = 2 856 J = 2.856 kJ. Moles of water formed = 0.050 × 1.0 = 0.050 mol. ΔH = −2.856 / 0.050 = −57.1 kJ/mol.

title: Hess's Law
summary: The statement of Hess's law, why it is true, and calculations with enthalpy cycles.

p: Hess's law of constant heat summation: the total enthalpy change of a reaction is the same whatever route is taken, provided the starting and finishing conditions are the same. It is true because enthalpy is a state function.
It lets us calculate ΔH for reactions that cannot be measured directly (such as carbon burning to carbon monoxide only, with no carbon dioxide), and heats of formation, combustion and atomisation.
Direct route: C(s) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g), ΔH = −394 kJ/mol.
Indirect route: C(s) + ½O₂(g) → CO(g), ΔH₁ = −110 kJ/mol; then CO(g) + ½O₂(g) → CO₂(g), ΔH₂ = −284 kJ/mol. Total = −110 + (−284) = −394 kJ/mol. The two routes agree.

sections.h: Worked example: formation of nitrogen monoxide
p: Find ΔH for N₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2NO(g), given (1) N₂(g) + 2O₂(g) → 2NO₂(g), ΔH = +66 kJ and (2) 2NO(g) + O₂(g) → 2NO₂(g), ΔH = −114 kJ.

Reverse equation (2): 2NO₂ → 2NO + O₂, ΔH = +114 kJ. Add it to (1): N₂ + 2O₂ + 2NO₂ → 2NO₂ + 2NO + O₂, which simplifies to N₂ + O₂ → 2NO. ΔH = +66 + 114 = +180 kJ. (Endothermic: this is why nitrogen oxides form in hot engines and in lightning.)

If you reverse an equation, change the sign of ΔH. If you multiply an equation by a number, multiply ΔH by the same number. Add the equations so that unwanted substances cancel, and add the ΔH values.

sections.h: Another example: using heats of combustion
p: Given the heats of combustion: C(s) −394 kJ/mol, H₂(g) −286 kJ/mol and CH₄(g) −890 kJ/mol, find the heat of formation of CH₄: C + 2H₂ → CH₄. ΔH = Σ(combustion of reactants) − Σ(combustion of products) = (−394) + 2(−286) − (−890) = −966 + 890 = −76 kJ/mol.

Calculating standard enthalpy changes; designing energy-efficient industrial processes; finding the energy (calorific) value of foods; understanding respiration and photosynthesis; judging whether a reaction is likely to happen.

title: Energetics: Activation Energy and Energy Profile Diagrams
summary: Bond breaking and bond making, activation energy, energy profile diagrams for exothermic and endothermic reactions and the effect of a catalyst.

p: In every reaction, bonds in the reactants are broken and new bonds form in the products. Breaking bonds takes in energy (endothermic). Making bonds gives out energy (exothermic). The overall ΔH is the balance. If more energy is released than taken in, the reaction is exothermic (ΔH negative). If more is taken in than released, it is endothermic (ΔH positive).

Activation energy (Eₐ) is the minimum energy that colliding particles must have to start a reaction. Think of it as a hill that the reactants must climb. Even exothermic reactions need it: a match must be struck before it burns. High Eₐ means a slow reaction (rusting). Low Eₐ means a fast reaction (neutralisation). A catalyst lowers Eₐ.
An energy profile shows the energy of the system as the reaction proceeds.

Exothermic: the reactants start higher. The curve rises to a peak (the height above the reactants is Eₐ) and then falls to the products, which are lower. The difference in level between reactants and products is ΔH (negative).
Endothermic: the reactants start lower. The curve rises to a peak and ends at products that are higher than the reactants. ΔH is positive.
Catalyst: the catalysed pathway has a lower peak. Eₐ is smaller, but the levels of the reactants and products, and so ΔH, are the same.

img.alt: Three energy profile diagrams: an exothermic reaction with products lower than reactants, an endothermic reaction with products higher than reactants, and the effect of a catalyst which lowers the peak
img.cap: Energy profiles for exothermic and endothermic reactions, and the effect of a catalyst.

p: Example 1. Eₐ = 150 kJ and ΔH = −75 kJ. ΔH is negative, so it is exothermic. The peak is 150 kJ above the reactants and the products are 75 kJ below the reactants. The activation energy of the reverse reaction is 150 + 75 = 225 kJ.
Example 2. ΔH = +120 kJ/mol and Eₐ = 200 kJ/mol. Endothermic. The peak is 200 kJ above the reactants; the products are 120 kJ above the reactants; the reverse Eₐ is 200 − 120 = 80 kJ/mol.
Example 3. H₂O₂ decomposes slowly because of a high activation energy. MnO₂ gives another pathway with lower Eₐ, so it decomposes quickly.

'Exothermic reactions need no activation energy': wrong; all reactions need some. 'A catalyst changes ΔH': wrong; it only lowers Eₐ. 'A faster reaction releases more heat': wrong; speed depends on Eₐ, heat released depends on ΔH. Rusting is slow although it is exothermic, because its activation energy is high.

Striking a match: friction supplies the activation energy. Respiration: enzymes lower the Eₐ of glucose oxidation. Cooking: heat supplies the activation energy. Industry: iron in the Haber process, vanadium(V) oxide in the Contact process and nickel in the hydrogenation of oils.
